content: 1. Postnatal HIV transmission rates at six and twelve months of age were analyzed in infants born to HIV-infected women who initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) and practiced breastfeeding. This analysis was conducted through a systematic review of the literature. 2. The 2010 WHO guidelines on infant feeding in the context of HIV recommended exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months, followed by complementary feeding and continued breastfeeding (CBF) up to one year, provided that either the mother or the infant was on ART. 3. At the time these guidelines were developed, there was limited data on the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in women who were on ART during pregnancy and continued ART postpartum, or in infants who received ART prophylaxis to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). 4. Over the past five years, additional evidence has emerged from studies and programs where PMTCT was achieved postnatally through maternal ART or infant antiretroviral (ARV) prophylaxis. 5. A key question remains regarding the potential increased risk of HIV transmission when infants receive mixed feeding (breast milk combined with other feeds) during the first six months of life. In the pre-ART and pre-PMTCT era, mixed feeding was associated with a significantly higher risk of HIV transmission. 6. In October 2015, the 2010 WHO guidelines on HIV and infant feeding were reviewed in light of the expanded use of ART in pregnant and breastfeeding women. 7. This review also sought to address whether maternal ART is effective in reducing the risk of postnatal HIV transmission even when mothers practice mixed feeding. 8. The systematic review presented here includes GRADE evidence summary tables and focuses on overall and postnatal HIV transmission rates at six, nine, twelve, and eighteen months in infants born to women on ART, stratified by infant feeding modality during the first six months of life. 9. The review also provides detailed information on infant feeding recommendations given to women in the included studies, which were conducted as randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and longitudinal studies involving HIV-positive mothers on ART and their breastfed infants. 10. Infants in these studies may have also received prophylactic ARVs as per the 2010 WHO guidelines. 11. The participants included HIV-positive mothers who initiated ART before or early in pregnancy and continued ART for at least six months postpartum, as well as their breastfed infants. 12. The exposures examined were maternal ART and the type of infant feeding during breastfeeding (exclusive breastfeeding versus mixed feeding). 13. The outcome measures included overall HIV transmission rates from birth to six months, postnatal transmission rates between four to six weeks and six months, and overall and postnatal transmission rates at twelve, eighteen, or twenty-four months. 14. The search strategy involved a comprehensive review of English-language literature from multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and CINAHL, covering the period from 2005 to 2015. 15. Search terms included combinations of keywords related to maternal ART, HIV transmission, and infant feeding practices, linked by Boolean operators. 16. The search identified 1,439 citations, of which 72 abstracts were screened, 35 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 11 studies were ultimately included in the systematic review. 17. Studies were excluded if they did not report transmission rates at six months, did not involve mothers on ART, or lacked detailed information on feeding modality and transmission outcomes. 18. The quality of the included studies was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which evaluated factors such as the representativeness of the study population, ascertainment of ART and feeding exposures, maternal adherence to ART, and the reporting of HIV transmission outcomes. 19. The GRADE framework was used to comment on the quality of evidence, considering study limitations, consistency of results, directness, precision, and reporting bias. 20. The synthesis of evidence included narrative summaries and pooled estimates of transmission rates, with heterogeneity scores calculated using random-effects meta-analysis. 21. Eleven studies were included, with four nested within randomized clinical trials. All studies involved mothers who initiated ART before or during pregnancy and continued ART for at least six months postpartum. 22. Eight studies followed the WHO recommendation of six-month ART, while three studies provided lifelong ART for all women or only for those eligible based on low CD4 counts. 23. The quality of the studies varied, with some achieving high scores for selection and outcome assessment. However, limitations included the lack of denominators for transmission rates stratified by feeding modality in some studies. 24. Postnatal HIV transmission rates were reported at six months in six studies, while five studies reported transmission rates beyond six months. Some studies provided detailed data on the number of infections and children at risk, while others did not. 25. The pooled estimate of overall HIV transmission rates at six months showed considerable heterogeneity between studies, with confidence intervals calculated where not provided. 26. The findings highlight the importance of maternal ART in reducing postnatal HIV transmission, even in the context of mixed feeding, and provide critical evidence for updating WHO guidelines on HIV and infant feeding.
